summary:
TerraPulse is a web platform that acts as a digital advisor for farmers facing water scarcity, soil degradation and extreme events. A farmer draws a field on an interactive map. The system pulls NASA data plus weather and terrain inputs. Four PyTorch neural networks then cover water stress, soil degradation, crop rotation and post-fire recovery. The output is plain-language advice: irrigation schedules, rotation plans, and post-fire rehabilitation protocols. It includes a What-If simulator, bilingual (Greek/English) interface, voice read-out and printable prescription sheet that make it usable without technical skills.

Field trials of sensor-based irrigation scheduling have cut water use by 27–45% with no yield loss, and legume rotations can fix 32–115 kg N/ha per year, reducing synthetic fertilizer needs by up to 40%. TerraPulse is built to bring these gains to ordinary farms. Existing tools deliver such benefits only in pieces: satellite platforms offer monitoring, public services supply raw data layers, and crop or erosion models demand specialist calibration. We found no tool that combines water management, soil health, rotation planning and post-fire recovery in one simple interface. TerraPulse does this, turning NASA data into clear, actionable advice that lets non-specialists save water, cut fertilizer costs and protect their income. Planned extensions include transformer/LSTM models, Sentinel-2 and NISAR data, and IoT-controlled irrigation.
details:
We built TerraPulse because farmers face unpredictable droughts, soil depletion, and extreme weather like wildfires without practical tools that tell them what to actually do in the field the next morning. Most existing platforms either show raw satellite layers that take GIS skills to interpret or focus only on basic monitoring. Our goal was to bridge that gap with a simple web-based digital advisor tailored to each individual parcel.

When a user opens TerraPulse, they start on an interactive 3D Earth showing orbital markers for NASA missions like SMAP and ECOSTRESS, then launch into a 2D map workspace where they can search any location worldwide and draw a polygon around their field. The platform automatically calculates the real geodesic area in hectares and stremmata, generates a heuristic grid showing drier and wetter sub-zones, and lets users save two parcels as Field A and Field B to compare them side by side. Those coordinates go to our Python FastAPI backend, which calculates the local terrain slope from five elevation points and pulls 30 days of past weather, a 7-day forecast (including reference evapotranspiration and precipitation), and 7-28 cm root-zone soil moisture from Open-Meteo, cached for 10 minutes. We combine those live feeds with crop coefficients, irrigation efficiencies (52% for flood, 74% for sprinkler, 93% for drip), and agro-climatic baselines and biophysical priors informed by NASA Earth Observation datasets (NASA POWER, SMAP, ECOSTRESS, GPM, Landsat, MODIS, and SRTM).

At startup, the backend loads four PyTorch neural networks that we developed as proof-of-concept surrogate models trained on synthetic agro-climatic datasets grounded in established physical equations (FAO-56 water balance, RUSLE erosion, biological nitrogen fixation benchmarks, and post-fire dNBR/erosion response curves). The first network is a 3-layer MLP (6 -> 16 -> 8 -> 1) that takes six aggregated 6-month features—temperature, rainfall, soil moisture, NDVI, slope, and evapotranspiration—to predict root-zone water stress and build a 7-day irrigation schedule that automatically skips days with at least 4 mm of rain. The second network scores soil and vegetation health alongside erosion risk to drive NPK balance, a soil biome radar, and cover-crop advice. The third evaluates rotation options like legumes, alfalfa, durum wheat, and sorghum, estimating biological nitrogen fixation and comparing 3-year profitability against monoculture. The fourth assesses post-fire erosion risk and vegetation recovery potential to produce a 12-month rebound curve, a 72-hour emergency cover-seeding plan, and an SMS alert preview.

What makes TerraPulse creative is how it brings four separate agronomic problems—irrigation, soil degradation, crop rotation, and post-disaster fire recovery—into one unified workspace with an interactive What-If Simulator. By switching the crop (wheat, cotton, corn, olives, vineyard, alfalfa), the irrigation method, or testing extreme conditions like a +5.5 °C heatwave or a post-fire storm, the farmer watches all four neural networks recalculate risks, water volumes, and costs in real time. The dashboard itself uses a two-layer layout: Layer 1 gives an immediate risk gauge and plain-language steps for the next morning, while Layer 2 opens up multi-series charts, water and fertilizer cost comparisons, and a full scientific report.

For development, we built the frontend in HTML, CSS, and JavaScript using Three.js for the 3D globe, Leaflet and Leaflet.Draw for mapping, OpenStreetMap Nominatim for location search, Chart.js for data visualization, and the browser's Web Speech API for voice readout. The backend runs on Python, FastAPI, and PyTorch, pulling live weather from Open-Meteo alongside NASA EO-informed model baselines. Everything runs in a standard browser and lightweight server without requiring specialized on-farm hardware, though the modular REST architecture is ready to connect to smart valves or field sensors in the future.

Throughout the project, our team focused heavily on real-world usability in rural areas. We made the entire interface—and all backend-generated schedules, charts, and scientific reports—fully bilingual between Greek and English with a single toggle. We added a Listen button that reads advice aloud for hands-free use in the field, a one-page ink-friendly PDF print layout for taking prescriptions outside, automatic pausing of the 3D globe inside the workspace to save GPU power, and a deterministic offline fallback so the app still works smoothly if external API connections drop.

By turning complex environmental modeling into simple daily decisions, TerraPulse is designed to cut wasted water, pumping electricity, and chemical fertilizer costs while protecting soils from erosion and climate shocks. Based on published field trials of comparable sensor-guided irrigation and legume-diversified rotations, the strategies built into TerraPulse align with projected savings of 27–45% in irrigation water without hurting yield, 32–115 kg N/ha/year from biological nitrogen fixation, and up to a 40% reduction in synthetic nitrogen fertilizer dependency—helping keep farms both environmentally resilient and economically viable.
